blocks.text: The opening identifies this work as an oracle concerning Nineveh and as a vision-book associated with Nahum the Elkoshite. Within the chapter, the portrayal of God as a refuge for those in distress (v. 7) stands alongside the closing announcement of good news and peace to Judah: the messenger’s news is linked with keeping festivals, fulfilling vows, and the end of the wicked oppressor (v. 15).

Several features of Nahum 1 remain debated. Verses 2–8 show possible alphabetic patterning, but scholars disagree about how complete or intentional an acrostic pattern may be. The movement of speech in verses 9–15 also shifts between hostile and consoling language, while the precise speakers and addressees are uncertain. The chapter can therefore be read attentively without treating every change of voice or arrangement as settled.

The chapter speaks intensely of divine vengeance and judgment against enemies. Responsible reception preserves the chapter’s hope for people harmed by empire while refusing to turn its language into antisemitism, ethnic proxy, misogyny, sexual violence, survivor blame, revenge, or justification for modern war.

In common English chapter numbering, the good-news announcement is Nahum 1:15. In the Masoretic chapter division, the same verse is numbered Nahum 2:1. This can explain why editions and commentaries sometimes cite the passage differently.
